stimulus.title: Columbus describes the Taíno, 1492
stimulus.text: They have no iron, their darts being wands without iron, some of them having a fish’s tooth at the end, and others being pointed in various ways. . . . They should be good servants and intelligent, for I observed that they quickly took in what was said to them, and I believe that they would easily be made Christians, as it appeared to me that they had no religion, our Lord being pleased, will take hence, at the time of my departure, six natives for your Highnesses that they may learn to speak.
stimulus.attribution: Christopher Columbus, journal entry, October 1492 (trans. Clements R. Markham, 1893)

questions.stem: Columbus’s assessment of the people he encountered most directly reflects which Spanish objectives in the Americas?
choices: Negotiating commercial treaties with Native states on equal terms
Establishing family farming settlements for religious dissenters
Converting Native peoples to Christianity and exploiting their labor
Acquiring Native agricultural knowledge to relieve food shortages in Spain
questions.explanation: Columbus pairs "good servants" with "easily be made Christians," anticipating the Spanish combination of coerced labor and missionary work. He treats the Taíno as subjects, not trading equals, and Spain did not send dissenting family settlers.

questions.stem: The encounters that began with the voyage described in the excerpt most directly caused which development during the following century?
choices: Catastrophic Native population decline, which encouraged Spain to import enslaved Africans
A rapid decline in Spanish power as American silver left Europe for Asia
The withdrawal of Portugal from its trading posts on the West African coast
The spread of Native American political institutions to European monarchies
questions.explanation: Epidemic disease and brutal labor regimes devastated Caribbean and mainland populations, and Spain increasingly turned to enslaved African labor. American bullion strengthened Spain in the sixteenth century rather than weakening it.

questions.stem: Which feature of the excerpt’s intended audience most likely shaped how Columbus described the island’s inhabitants?
choices: He wrote for Church scholars who were debating whether Native people could be enslaved
He hoped to discourage rival Spanish explorers from seeking licenses of their own
He was defending himself to colonists who had accused him of mismanaging Hispaniola
He needed to convince his royal sponsors that the lands he reached would repay further investment
questions.explanation: The journal addresses "your Highnesses," Ferdinand and Isabella, whose backing Columbus needed. Stressing docile, convertible people served that purpose. The debates over enslavement and the complaints about his governorship came later.

stimulus.title: Las Casas on Spanish conduct in the Indies, 1542
stimulus.text: Now the ultimate end and scope that incited the Spaniards to endeavor the Extirpation and Desolation of this People, was Gold only… Finally, in one word, their Ambition and Avarice, than which the heart of Man never entertained greater, and the vast Wealth of those Regions; the Humility and Patience of the Inhabitants (which made their approach to these Lands more easy) did much promote the business: Whom they so despicably contemned, that they treated them (I speak of things which I was an Eye Witness of, without the least fallacy) not as Beasts, which I cordially wished they would, but as the most abject dung and filth of the Earth
stimulus.attribution: Bartolomé de las Casas, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies, written 1542 (English translation, 1689)

questions.stem: The abuses Las Casas describes were most closely associated with which Spanish colonial institution?
choices: The mission system, which gathered Native converts under the supervision of friars
The encomienda system, which granted colonists the labor and tribute of Native communities
The asiento, which licensed foreign merchants to deliver enslaved Africans
The casta system, which ranked colonial subjects by ancestry
questions.explanation: Encomenderos received rights to Native labor and tribute, which produced the exploitation Las Casas condemned. Missions, the asiento, and casta classification were features of the empire but are not the labor regime he is attacking here.

questions.stem: Arguments like those in the excerpt contributed most directly to which action by the Spanish crown?
choices: Ending the transatlantic slave trade to Spanish colonies
Issuing the New Laws of 1542, which attempted to restrict the enslavement of Native people and limit encomiendas
Granting self-government to Native communities in New Spain
Abandoning efforts to convert Native peoples to Catholicism
questions.explanation: The New Laws tried to curb Native slavery and phase out encomiendas, though colonists resisted and enforcement was weak. The crown expanded African slavery and never abandoned conversion or granted Native self-rule.

questions.stem: English writers in the late 1500s and 1600s translated and reprinted accounts like this one mainly in order to
choices: persuade Parliament to prohibit English participation in the slave trade
argue that England should avoid colonization because it corrupted colonizers
encourage English Catholics to settle in Spanish America
portray Spanish colonization as uniquely cruel and thereby justify English challenges to Spain
questions.explanation: Protestant rivals used Las Casas to build the "Black Legend" of Spanish cruelty, which cast English expansion as a righteous alternative. England did not restrict its slave trade until 1807 and was not deterred from colonizing.

questions.stem: Defenders of Spanish colonial practices, such as Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, answered arguments like those in the excerpt by claiming that
choices: Native peoples were naturally inferior, which justified conquering them and compelling their labor
Spain should withdraw from the Americas
Native peoples already practiced Christianity
the crown had no authority over colonists
questions.explanation: In the Valladolid debate of 1550–1551, Sepúlveda argued that Native people were "natural slaves" who benefited from Spanish rule, while Las Casas defended their humanity and rights.

stimulus.title: Hakluyt argues for English colonization, 1584
stimulus.text: That this western discoverie will be greatly for the enlargement of the gospel of Christ whereunto the Princes of the reformed religion are chiefly bound amongst whom her Majestie is principally. . . . That this western voyage will yield unto us all the commodities of Europe, Africa, and Asia, as far as we were wont to travel, and supply the wants of all our decayed trades. That this enterprise will be for the manifold employment of numbers of idle men . . . That this voyage will be a great bridle to the Indies of the king of Spaine
stimulus.attribution: Richard Hakluyt, Discourse of Western Planting, written for Queen Elizabeth I, 1584

questions.stem: Hakluyt’s reference to "the Princes of the reformed religion" and to a "bridle" on the king of Spain is best understood in the context of
choices: English efforts to form a military alliance with Spain against France
disputes between the English crown and Puritans over church governance
religious and imperial rivalry between Protestant England and Catholic Spain
papal approval of English claims to North America
questions.explanation: Hakluyt frames colonization as a Protestant duty and a strategic blow against Spain, England’s chief rival in the 1580s. England and Spain were moving toward war, not alliance, and the papacy had divided the Americas between Spain and Portugal.

questions.stem: Hakluyt’s claim that colonization would provide "employment of numbers of idle men" most directly reflects which condition in sixteenth-century England?
choices: A labor shortage caused by recurring outbreaks of plague
The emigration of skilled artisans to Spanish colonies
A decline in the wool trade caused by competition from American cotton
Population growth and the enclosure of farmland, which left many laborers without work
questions.explanation: Rising population and enclosure displaced rural workers, and promoters presented colonies as an outlet for the unemployed poor. England faced surplus labor, not a shortage, and American cotton was not yet a commercial rival.

questions.stem: Compared with the Spanish colonies established in the sixteenth century, the English colonies eventually founded in North America differed most in that they
choices: depended primarily on tribute collected from densely populated Native empires
were governed directly by royal viceroys appointed in London
attracted larger numbers of settlers who came to farm and who lived apart from Native peoples
prohibited the private companies that financed exploration
questions.explanation: English colonies drew comparatively many migrants, including families, who sought land and generally excluded rather than incorporated Native people. Tribute and viceroys describe Spanish rule, and English ventures relied on joint-stock companies.

stimulus.title: The Coronado expedition besieges a Pueblo town, 1540–1541
stimulus.text: The siege lasted fifty days, during which time several assaults were made. The lack of water was what troubled the Indians most. . . . It was impossible to persuade them to make peace, as they said that the Spaniards would not keep an agreement made with them. . . . Don Lope begged them to make peace, giving them the strongest promises for their safety. They told him to go away, as they did not wish to trust themselves to people who had no regard for friendship or their own word which they had pledged.
stimulus.attribution: Pedro de Castañeda, narrative of the Coronado expedition (trans. George Parker Winship, 1898)

questions.stem: The fortified town that withstood a fifty-day siege in the excerpt best illustrates which characteristic of Native societies in the Southwest before European contact?
choices: Seasonal camps organized around the pursuit of bison herds on horseback
Permanent settlements supported by maize cultivation in an arid environment
Dispersed fishing villages dependent on coastal resources
Large cities that collected tribute from conquered provinces
questions.explanation: Pueblo peoples built compact, permanent towns sustained by maize agriculture and careful water management. Horse-mounted bison hunting came after Spanish contact, and coastal fishing and tribute empires describe other regions.

questions.stem: Expeditions such as the one described in the excerpt were undertaken primarily because Spaniards
choices: hoped to find wealthy societies comparable to those conquered in Mexico and Peru
sought farmland for the surplus population of Spain
intended to open a fur trade with northern Native nations
wanted to block English settlement along the Atlantic coast
questions.explanation: After the conquests of the Aztec and Inca empires, rumors of rich cities drew Coronado north. Spain was not seeking farmland for emigrants or furs, and no English colony yet existed to block.

questions.stem: The distrust expressed by the besieged in the excerpt foreshadowed which later development in the same region?

stimulus.title: Cabeza de Vaca among the Avavares, 1530s
stimulus.text: We remained with the Avavares Indians for eight months, according to our reckoning of the moons. questions.stem: Which of the following contributed most to the growth of the total population between 1700 and 1750?
choices: High birth rates together with immigration from Germany, Scotland, and Ireland
The annexation of French settlements in Canada
A sharp increase in migration from Spain
The arrival of most of the Puritan migrants from England
questions.explanation: The colonial population roughly doubled every generation through natural increase, supplemented by German and Scots-Irish migrants. The Puritan migration was concentrated in the 1630s, and Canada remained French until 1763.

questions.stem: By 1750 the trend in total population shown in the chart had contributed most directly to
choices: a decline in colonial trade with Britain
the end of the headright system in New England
settlers pushing into the backcountry, which increased conflict with Native peoples and with France
colonial demands for independence from Britain
questions.explanation: A fast-growing population sought land west of the coastal settlements, producing friction in the Ohio Valley that helped bring on the Seven Years’ War. Trade with Britain was growing, and calls for independence came later.

stimulus.title: Pontiac relates the teachings of Neolin, 1763
stimulus.text: This land, where you live, I have made for you and not for others. How comes it that you suffer the whites on your lands? Can you not do without them? . . . You might live wholly as you did before you knew them. Before those whom you call your brothers come on your lands, did you not live by bow and arrow? You had no need of gun nor powder, nor the rest of their things . . . but as regards those who have come to trouble your country, drive them out, make war on them.
stimulus.attribution: Pontiac, Ottawa leader, recounting the message of the Delaware prophet Neolin, 1763

questions.stem: The call to action in the excerpt was most directly a response to
choices: the Proclamation of 1763, which opened the Ohio Valley to colonial settlement
the Stamp Act, which taxed trade goods sold to Native peoples
the founding of Spanish missions in the lower Mississippi Valley
Britain’s victory in the Seven Years’ War, which removed France as a counterweight in the Great Lakes region
questions.explanation: With France defeated, Native nations could no longer play empires against one another, and British officers cut customary gifts while settlers pressed west. The Proclamation followed the uprising and restricted settlement.

questions.stem: The uprising associated with the excerpt most directly prompted the British government to
choices: withdraw all British troops from North America
recognize an independent Native confederacy in the Ohio Valley
prohibit colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains
repeal the Navigation Acts
questions.explanation: Hoping to avoid costly frontier wars, Britain issued the Proclamation of 1763 reserving the trans-Appalachian West for Native nations. The army remained in America, which became a source of colonial grievance.

questions.stem: The message in the excerpt most closely resembles which later movement?
choices: The Cherokee adoption of a written constitution and plantation agriculture
The effort of Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa to unite Native nations and reject American goods and land cessions
The decision of some Iroquois nations to ally with Britain during the Revolution
The acceptance of allotment by leaders seeking United States citizenship
questions.explanation: Like Neolin and Pontiac, Tenskwatawa preached spiritual renewal and separation from European ways while Tecumseh built a pan-Indian alliance. The Cherokee strategy selectively adopted American institutions instead.

stimulus.text: But there is another and great distinction for which no truly natural or religious reason can be assigned, and that is the distinction of men into KINGS and SUBJECTS. Male and female are the distinctions of nature, good and bad the distinctions of Heaven; but how a race of men came into the world so exalted above the rest, and distinguished like some new species, is worth inquiring into . . . questions.stem: Paine’s argument marked a departure from most earlier colonial protests because it
choices: rejected monarchy itself rather than blaming Parliament and the king’s ministers
asked for colonial representation in the House of Commons
defended the rights of the colonists as Englishmen under the British constitution
proposed that the colonies accept taxation in exchange for western land
questions.explanation: Before 1776 most colonists professed loyalty to George III and blamed Parliament or corrupt ministers. Paine attacked hereditary rule as illegitimate, making reconciliation under the crown unthinkable.

questions.stem: Which feature of the excerpt best explains why Common Sense reached a far wider audience than most political pamphlets of its time?
choices: It relied on Latin quotations and detailed analysis of English legal precedent
It was written anonymously by a well-known member of the colonial elite
It used plain language and biblical references familiar to ordinary colonists
It avoided criticizing the king in order to appeal to moderates
questions.explanation: Paine wrote in direct prose and argued from scripture, which most colonists knew, rather than from learned legal citation. He was a recent immigrant of modest background, and he attacked the king openly.

choices: Members of the Sons of Liberty
Delegates who signed the Declaration of Independence
French officials who hoped to weaken Britain

questions.explanation: Perhaps a fifth of colonists remained loyal to the crown, among them royal officials, many Anglican clergy, and merchants with British connections.

questions.stem: Abigail Adams’s warning that women "will not hold ourselves bound by any Laws in which we have no voice, or Representation" most directly

restates the doctrine of virtual representation
rejects the natural-rights philosophy of the Enlightenment
questions.explanation: She turns "no taxation without representation" on the patriots themselves, arguing that consent should extend to women. Virtual representation was the British defense of taxing the colonies, the opposite of her point.

questions.stem: The "unlimited power" of husbands that the excerpt criticizes refers most directly to
choices: primogeniture, under which estates passed to the eldest son
coverture, under which a married woman’s legal identity and property were controlled by her husband
statutes that barred women from membership in churches
colonial laws that required women to marry by a certain age
questions.explanation: Under the common-law doctrine of coverture, a wife could not own property, make contracts, or sue independently. Primogeniture concerned inheritance among sons, and women were full church members.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how women’s status changed in the decades immediately after the letter was written?
choices: Most states granted property-owning women the right to vote
Coverture was abolished by the new state constitutions
Women were admitted to colleges and the professions on equal terms
Women gained no formal political rights, but "republican motherhood" encouraged expanded female education
questions.explanation: The Revolution left coverture and male suffrage intact, yet the idea that mothers must raise virtuous citizens justified new academies for girls. Only New Jersey briefly allowed some women to vote.

stimulus.title: Washington warns against party spirit, 1796
stimulus.text: Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally. This spirit, unfortunately, is inseparable from our nature, having its root in the strongest passions of the human mind. . . . The alternate domination of one faction over another, sharpened by the spirit of revenge, natural to party dissension, which in different ages and countries has perpetrated the most horrid enormities, is itself a frightful despotism.
stimulus.attribution: George Washington, Farewell Address, 1796

questions.stem: Washington’s warning was prompted most directly by disagreements during his presidency over

the admission of Missouri as a slave state

the constitutionality of the Louisiana Purchase
questions.explanation: Federalists and Democratic-Republicans had formed around Hamilton’s bank, debt, and tax policies and around whether to favor Britain or France. Missouri and Louisiana came later, and the Articles had already been replaced.

questions.stem: Washington’s view of faction differs from the argument James Madison made in The Federalist No. 10 in that Madison

questions.explanation: Madison agreed that faction was rooted in human nature but held that an extended republic would keep any single faction from dominating. Neither man welcomed permanent parties, and Madison rejected curbing liberty as a remedy.

stimulus.text: In our day it appears as the struggle of freemen to gain and hold the right of self-government as against the special interests, who twist the methods of free government into machinery for defeating the popular will. questions.stem: After 2008, critics of the law described in the excerpt argued that it had

reduced the size of the largest financial institutions
questions.explanation: The housing collapse and the failure or rescue of major firms in 2008 renewed calls for regulation, and Congress passed the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010. Historians and economists still debate how much the 1999 law mattered.

The 1790s, when Congress first defined citizenship
The 1910s and 1920s, when a high level of immigration prompted demands for restriction
The 1950s, when most Americans supported existing quotas
